It is Meccan according to the opinion of Ibn Mas'ud, Jabir, al-Hasan, Ikrimah and 'Ata', and Madani according to the opinion of Ibn 'Abbas, Anas ibn Malik and Qatadah.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Al-'Adiyat is the plural of 'adiyah, which means that which runs swiftly, from al-'adw, which is walking swiftly. The waw was changed to a ya' because of the kasrah before it, like al-ghaziyat from al-ghazw. What is meant by it is the war horses that run in battle, like running (al-'adw). His saying "dabhan" (ضبحا) is a verbal noun (masdar) emphasizing the active participle, for dabh is a kind of travel and a kind of running. It is said "dabaha al-faras" when the horse runs with force; it is taken from al-dab' (ضبع), which means pushing, and it seems that the ha' is a substitute for the 'ayn.

Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Mubarrad said: dabh comes from the horse stretching its legs (ida'uha) in travel, and from this is the saying of 'Antarah:

"And the horses churn in the pools of death, dabhan"

It may be a masdar in the position of a circumstantial accusative (hal): i.e., dabihat (panting), or possessing dabh. It may also be a masdar of a deleted verb: i.e., they pant a panting. It is said that dabh is the sound of their hooves when they run. Al-Farra' said: dabh is the sound of the horses' breathing when they run.

It is said: they used to muzzle them so that they would not neigh and the enemy would learn of them, so they used to breathe forcefully in this state. It is also said that dabh is a sound heard from the chests of horses when running, which is not neighing (sahil).

The majority has gone to what we mentioned, that the al-'adiyat dabhan are horses. 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, Muhammad ibn Ka'b and al-Suddi said: they are camels, and from this is the saying of Safiyyah bint 'Abd al-Muttalib:

"By the running ones at the gathering of Jam', with their hands, when the dust bursts forth"

The lexicographers reported that the original meaning of dabh belongs to the fox, and it was borrowed for horses. From this is the saying of the poet:

"It pants in the palm like the panting of a fox"

﴿By those that strike sparks by striking﴾ are the horses when they strike fire with their hooves. Al-iraa' is bringing out fire, and al-qadah is striking; the horses' striking with their hooves is made like the striking of flint with steel.

Al-Zajjaj said: when horses run at night and their hooves are struck by stones, sparks fly out of them. The discussion on the accusative of qadhan is like the discussion on the accusative of dabhan, and the disagreement over whether they are horses or camels is like the disagreement mentioned earlier concerning al-'adiyat.

The preponderant view is that they are horses, as the majority held, and as is apparent from the descriptions mentioned in this surah, both what precedes and what follows, for they are clearer in the case of horses than of camels. What differences exist on this among the Companions will come later.

﴿By those that raid at dawn﴾, i.e., those that attack the enemy at morning time. It is said: aghara yughiru ighratan, when he surprises his enemy with killing, capture or plunder. The raiding is attributed to them though it belongs to their people, to indicate that they are their main force in raiding. The accusative of subhan is as an adverb of time.

﴿Then raise thereby a cloud of dust﴾ is coordinated with the verb indicated by the active participle, since the meaning is: those who ran, then they raised; or coordinated with the active participle itself, because it is in the sense of a verb, occurring as a relative clause, for alif and lam in the attributes are relative pronouns. So the sense is: those who ran, then struck fire, then raided, then raised. Al-naq' is the dust they raise against the enemy's face at the time of the raid. Restricting its raising to the morning is because it is the time of the raid, and because the trace of the dust does not appear at night, which is adjacent to the morning.

It is also said that the meaning is: they raised dust in the place of their running, meaning: dust rose or they stirred it up.

The majority read fa-athrna with a light thā' (تخفيف المثلثة). Abu Haywah and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read with shaddah, i.e., they made dust appear thereby.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: al-naq' is raising the voice, and he quoted the verse of Labid:

"So when a true cry is raised, they summon them with jingling and clamour"

He means: when they hear a cry, they rouse the war, i.e., they gather for it.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: and on this I have seen the view of most people of knowledge. End.

But the known meaning among the majority of lexicographers and exegetes is that al-naq' is dust. From this is the saying of the poet:

"They emerge from scattered dust, wounded, as if the tips of their tails were tips of pens"

And the saying of 'Abd Allah ibn Rawahah:

"We would lose our horses if you did not see them stirring dust from the two sides of Kada'"

And the saying of another:

"As if the place of raised dust above our heads and our swords were a night whose stars are falling"

(p-1648) This is what suits the meaning of the verse. Interpreting naq' as sound has little meaning here, for your saying "the horses raided the people of so-and-so at morning and thereby raised a sound" is of little benefit, meaningless, and far from the miraculous eloquence of the Qur'an.

It is also said that al-naq' is the tearing of garments. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: al-naq' is what lies between Muzdalifah and Mina. It is also said it is the bed of the valley.

In al-Sihah: al-naq' is dust, its plural is anqa'; al-naq' is a place where water is held, and likewise what gathers in a well; and al-naq' is land of clayey soil in which water stands.

﴿Then burst thereby into the midst of a host﴾, i.e., they penetrated at that time, or they penetrated, mixed with the dust, into a host of the enemy's hosts, or by their running they came into the midst of the enemy's host. The ba' is either for transitivity, or for circumstance (hal), or is extra. It is said wasatta al-makan: I came to be in its middle. The accusative of jam'an is as its object. The fa's in the four positions indicate the sequence of what follows each one upon what precedes it.

Al-Jumhur read fa-wasatna with a light sin, and it was also read with a shaddah.

﴿Indeed, mankind is ungrateful to his Lord﴾. This is the answer to the oath. What is meant by mankind is some of its members, namely the disbeliever. Al-kanud is one who is ungrateful for blessings. "Ungrateful toward the favours of men, and whoever is ungrateful toward the favours of men will be far"

i.e., ungrateful for the favours of men. It is said he is one who denies the truth; it is said that Kindah was so named because it denied its father.

It is also said that kanud is derived from kanad, which is cutting, as if he cut off what he should have kept connected of gratitude. It is said: kanada al-habl, when he cut the rope, and from this is the saying of al-A'sha:

"The joining of ropes and their cutting"

It is also said: al-kanud is the miser, and Abu Zayd recited:

"Indeed my soul has not been pleased with you, a soul, except that I am left with a debt that is ungrateful"

It is also said: al-kanud is the envious, and it is said the ignorant of his own worth. Interpreting kanud as ungrateful for blessings is more fitting to the context, and one who denies blessings is an unbeliever in them; the rest of what has been said does not suit the context.

It is also said the meaning is: indeed Allah, may His praise be exalted, is a witness to that from the son of Adam. The majority held this.

Al-Hasan, Qatadah and Muhammad ibn Ka'b held the first view.

And it is more preponderant than the view of the majority, because of His saying: ﴿And indeed he is, in love of wealth, intense﴾, for the pronoun refers to mankind. The meaning: indeed he is, in love of wealth, strong, diligent in seeking and acquiring it, and absorbed in it. It is said: he is intense (shadid) for this matter and strong for it when he is capable of it. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If he leaves wealth (khayr)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 180], and from this is the saying of 'Adi ibn Hatim:

"What do souls hope for from seeking the good, and love of life is its liar"

It is also said: the meaning is: indeed mankind, because of love of wealth, is stingy. The first is preferable.

The lam in al-hubb is connected to shadid.

Ibn Zayd said: Allah called wealth "good" (khayr), though it may be evil, but people find it good, so He called it good.

Al-Farra' said: the original structure of the verse would be: "indeed he is intensely loving of the good," like His saying: ﴿On a stormy day﴾ [Ibrahim: 18], where stormy belongs to the wind, not the day; as if He said: on a day stormy for the wind.

﴿Does he not know that when what is in the graves is scattered﴾. The interrogative is for denial, and the fa' is for coordination upon an implied element required by the context: i.e., he does what he does of ugly deeds and yet does not know. Ba'thara means nathara and bahatha: i.e., what is in the graves of the dead is scattered and searched, and they are brought out.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: ba'thartu al-mata'a: I made its bottom its top.

Al-Farra' said: I heard some Arabs of Banu Asad say: bahthara, with ha' in place of 'ayn. This has been discussed before in His saying: ﴿And when the graves are scattered﴾ [al-Infitar: 4].

﴿And what is in the breasts is made apparent﴾, i.e., what is in them of good and evil is distinguished and clarified. Tahsil is distinguishing, so said the exegetes. It is also said: hussila means: uburiza (brought forth).

Al-Jumhur read hussila with a damma on the ha' and a shaddah on the sad, kasrah, in passive form. 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Yahya ibn Ya'mar and Nasr ibn 'Asim read hasala with fatha on the ha' and sad, lightened, in active form: i.e., it became apparent.

﴿Indeed their Lord, concerning them, that Day, is All-Aware﴾, i.e., indeed the Lord of those who are resurrected, concerning them, is All-Aware; nothing of them is hidden from Him, so He will recompense them: good for good, and evil for evil.

Al-Zajjaj said: Allah is aware of them on that day and on other days, but the meaning is: Allah will recompense them for their disbelief on that day. Similar is His saying: ﴿Those are they whom Allah knows what is in their hearts﴾ [al-Nisa': 63], meaning: those whose recompense Allah does not neglect.

Al-Jumhur read inna rabbahum with a kasrah on the hamzah and the lam in khabir. Abu al-Simak read with a fatha on the hamzah and dropped the lam from khabir.

Al-Bazzar, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Daraqutni in al-Afrad, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent out horsemen, and their news was delayed for a month, and no report came to him from them; so Allah revealed: ﴿By the running ones, panting (dabhan)﴾ — they panted with their feet." The wording of Ibn Mardawayh: they panted with their nostrils.

﴿By those that strike sparks by striking﴾: they struck stones with their hooves and brought forth fire. ﴿By those that raid at dawn﴾: they attacked the people at morning with a raid. ﴿Then raise thereby a cloud of dust﴾: they raised dust with their hooves. ﴿Then burst thereby into the midst of a host﴾: they attacked the whole people at morning.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated through another route from him, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent a detachment against the enemy, and its news was delayed, which grieved him; so Allah informed him of their news and what had happened to them, and He said: ﴿By the running ones, panting (dabhan)﴾ — he said: they are horses."

Dabh is the snorting of horses when they snort.

﴿By those that strike sparks by striking﴾ — he said: when the horses run, they strike fire as their hooves hit stones. ﴿By those that raid at dawn﴾ — he said: they are horses that raided, attacking the enemy at morning. ﴿Then raise thereby a cloud of dust﴾ — he said: they are horses that raised dust with their hooves, meaning by the running of horses; and al-naq' is dust. ﴿Then burst thereby into the midst of a host﴾ — he said: the host is the enemy.

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Abu Salih who said: I disputed with Ikrimah concerning the meaning of al-'adiyat. He said: Ibn 'Abbas said: they are horses in battle, and their panting is when they loosen their muzzles as they run. ﴿By those that strike sparks by striking﴾ — he said: they make the polytheists see their plot. ﴿By those that raid at dawn﴾ — he said: when they attack the enemy at morning. ﴿Then burst thereby into the midst of a host﴾ — he said: when they penetrate the middle of the enemy.

Abu Salih said: So I said: 'Ali said: they are camels in the pilgrimage, and my master was more knowing than your master.

The commentator (al-Shawkani) cites Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Anbari in *Kitab al-Adداد* (the Book of Opposites), and al-Hakim, who graded it sound, and Ibn Mardawayh, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "While I was sitting in the Hijr, a man came to me and asked about *al-'Adiyat dabha* (﴿the chargers, panting﴾). I said: 'They are the horses when they raid in the way of God, then they return at night, and they prepare their food and kindle their fire.' He turned away from me and went to Ali ibn Abi Talib, who was sitting beneath the water-spout of Zamzam, and asked him about *al-'Adiyat dabha*. Ali said: 'Did you ask anyone about it before me?' He said: 'Yes, I asked Ibn Abbas, and he said: they are the horses when they raid in the way of God.' Ali said: 'Go and call him to me.' When I stood over his head, he said: 'You give fatwas to people about what you have no knowledge of! By God, the first military expedition in Islam was Badr, and we had only two horses with us: a horse of al-Zubayr and a horse of al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad. So how can *al-'Adiyat dabha* be horses? *Al-'Adiyat dabha* are from 'Arafah to Muzdalifah, and when they reach Muzdalifah they kindle fires. *Al-Mughirat subha* are from Muzdalifah to Mina, and that is the gathering (jam').' As for His saying ﴿so they raise dust thereby﴾, it is the dust of the earth which they trample with their hooves and their shoes."

Ibn Abbas said: "So I retracted my statement and returned to what Ali had said."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Ibn Mas'ud regarding ﴿by the chargers, panting﴾ that he said: "They are the camels." They recorded it from him through al-A'mash from Ibrahim al-Nakha'i.

Ibrahim said: "Ali ibn Abi Talib also said: they are the camels."

Ibn Abbas said: "They are the horses." It reached Ali that Ibn Abbas said this, and he said: "We did not have any horses on the day of Badr."

Ibn Abbas said: "That was only in a small expedition (sariyyah) that was dispatched."

Abd ibn Humayd recorded from Amir al-Sha'bi that he said: "Ali and Ibn Abbas disputed about *al-'Adiyat dabha*. Ibn Abbas said: 'They are the horses.' Ali said: 'You lie, O son of Fulanah! By God, there was no rider with us on the day of Badr except al-Miqdad, who was on a piebald horse.'" He said: "And [Ali] used to say: they are the camels. Ibn Abbas said: 'Do you not see that they raise dust? Nothing raises dust except with its hooves.'"

Abd ibn Humayd and al-Hakim, who graded it sound, recorded through Mujahid from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿by the chargers, panting﴾ that he said: "The horses." ﴿Then those who strike sparks﴾: "A man when he strikes his flint." ﴿Then those who raid at dawn﴾: "The horses attacking the enemy at dawn." ﴿So they raise dust thereby﴾: "The dust." ﴿And cleave thereby into the midst of a host﴾: "The enemy."

Abd ibn Humayd recorded from Mujahid regarding ﴿by the chargers, panting﴾ that he said: Ibn Abbas said: "It is fighting." And Ibn Mas'ud said: "It is the Hajj."

Abd al-Razzaq, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded through Amr ibn Dinar from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿by the chargers, panting﴾ that he said: "No animal pants (yadbahu) except the dog or the horse." ﴿Then those who strike sparks﴾: "It is the plotting of a man who strikes and kindles." ﴿Then those who raid at dawn﴾: "The raid of horses at dawn." ﴿So they raise dust thereby﴾: "Dust, the sound of horses' hooves." ﴿And cleave thereby into the midst of a host﴾: "The gathering of the enemy."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿by the chargers, panting﴾ that he said: "The horses. Their panting is their snorting. Do you not see that when the horse runs it says 'ah ah'? That is its panting."

Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from Ali that he said: "The panting of horses is the *hamhamah* (a low neighing), and of camels is the *nafas* (breathing)."

Ibn Jarir recorded from Ibn Mas'ud regarding ﴿by the chargers, panting﴾ that he said: "They are the camels on the Hajj." ﴿Then those who strike sparks﴾: "When they sweep the pebbles with their soles, so that the pebbles strike one another and fire comes out of them." ﴿Then those who raid at dawn﴾: "When they pour forth from Jam'." ﴿So they raise dust thereby﴾: "When they go, they raise the dust."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh recorded through several chains from Ibn Abbas that he said: "*Al-kanud* in our language is the people of the town, the ungrateful one (al-kafur)."

Ibn Asakir recorded from Abu Umamah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding His saying ﴿Indeed, mankind is to his Lord ungrateful (kanud)﴾, that he said: "It means ungrateful (kafur)."

Abd ibn Humayd, al-Bukhari in *al-Adab*, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Mardawayh recorded from Abu Umamah that he said: "The *kanud* is the one who withholds his gift, travels alone, and beats his servant."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Daylami and Ibn Asakir also narrated this from him as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet) report. Al-Suyuti graded its chain as weak, and in its chain is Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, who is matruk (abandoned, of disregarded narrations). The mawquf (stopping at the companion) version is more sound, because it did not come through that chain.

Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿And indeed he is, to that, a witness﴾ that he said: "The man." ﴿And indeed he is, in love of wealth, intense﴾: "The wealth."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from him regarding ﴿When what is in the graves is scattered﴾ that he said: "Searched out." ﴿And what is in the breasts is obtained﴾: "Made manifest."

It is also said that kanud is derived from kanad, which is cutting, as if he cut off what he should have kept connected of gratitude. It is said: kanada al-habl, when he cut the rope, and from this is the saying of al-A'sha:

"The joining of ropes and their cutting"

It is also said: al-kanud is the miser, and Abu Zayd recited:

It is also said: al-kanud is the envious, and it is said the ignorant of his own worth. Interpreting kanud as ungrateful for blessings is more fitting to the context, and one who denies blessings is an unbeliever in them; the rest of what has been said does not suit the context.

﴿And indeed he is, to that, a witness﴾, i.e., indeed mankind, in his ingratitude, is a witness, testifying against himself by it, because its effect is apparent upon him. It is also said the meaning is: indeed Allah, may His praise be exalted, is a witness to that from the son of Adam. The majority held this.

Al-Hasan, Qatadah and Muhammad ibn Ka'b held the first view.

And it is more preponderant than the view of the majority, because of His saying: ﴿And indeed he is, in love of wealth, intense﴾, for the pronoun refers to mankind. The meaning: indeed he is, in love of wealth, strong, diligent in seeking and acquiring it, and absorbed in it. It is said: he is intense (shadid) for this matter and strong for it when he is capable of it. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If he leaves wealth (khayr)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 180], and from this is the saying of 'Adi ibn Hatim:

Ibn Zayd said: Allah called wealth "good" (khayr), though it may be evil, but people find it good, so He called it good.

﴿Does he not know that when what is in the graves is scattered﴾. Ba'thara means nathara and bahatha: i.e., what is in the graves of the dead is scattered and searched, and they are brought out.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: ba'thartu al-mata'a: I made its bottom its top.

Al-Jumhur read hussila with a damma on the ha' and a shaddah on the sad, kasrah, in passive form. 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Yahya ibn Ya'mar and Nasr ibn 'Asim read hasala with fatha on the ha' and sad, lightened, in active form: i.e., it became apparent.

Similar is His saying: ﴿Those are they whom Allah knows what is in their hearts﴾ [al-Nisa': 63], meaning: those whose recompense Allah does not neglect.

Al-Jumhur read inna rabbahum with a kasrah on the hamzah and the lam in khabir. Abu al-Simak read with a fatha on the hamzah and dropped the lam from khabir.

Al-Bazzar, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Daraqutni in al-Afrad, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent out horsemen, and their news was delayed for a month, and no report came to him from them; so Allah revealed: ﴿By the running ones, panting (dabhan)﴾ — they panted with their feet." The wording of Ibn Mardawayh: they panted with their nostrils.

﴿By those that strike sparks by striking﴾: they struck stones with their hooves and brought forth fire. ﴿By those that raid at dawn﴾: they attacked the people at morning with a raid. ﴿Then raise thereby a cloud of dust﴾: they raised dust with their hooves. ﴿Then burst thereby into the midst of a host﴾: they attacked the whole people at morning.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated through another route from him, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent a detachment against the enemy, and its news was delayed, which grieved him; so Allah informed him of their news and what had happened to them, and He said: ﴿By the running ones, panting (dabhan)﴾ — he said: they are horses."

Dabh is the snorting of horses when they snort.

﴿By those that strike sparks by striking﴾ — he said: when the horses run, they strike fire as their hooves hit stones. ﴿By those that raid at dawn﴾ — he said: they are horses that raided, attacking the enemy at morning. ﴿Then raise thereby a cloud of dust﴾ — he said: they are horses that raised dust with their hooves, meaning by the running of horses; and al-naq' is dust. ﴿Then burst thereby into the midst of a host﴾ — he said: the host is the enemy.

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Abu Salih who said: I disputed with Ikrimah concerning the meaning of al-'adiyat. He said: Ibn 'Abbas said: they are horses in battle, and their panting is when they loosen their muzzles as they run. ﴿By those that strike sparks by striking﴾ — he said: they make the polytheists see their plot. ﴿By those that raid at dawn﴾ — he said: when they attack the enemy at morning. ﴿Then burst thereby into the midst of a host﴾ — he said: when they penetrate the middle of the enemy.

Abu Salih said: So I said: 'Ali said: they are camels in the pilgrimage, and my master was more knowing than your master.

The commentator (al-Shawkani) cites Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Anbari in *Kitab al-Adداد* (the Book of Opposites), and al-Hakim, who graded it sound, and Ibn Mardawayh, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "While I was sitting in the Hijr, a man came to me and asked about *al-'Adiyat dabha* (﴿the chargers, panting﴾). I said: 'They are the horses when they raid in the way of God, then they return at night, and they prepare their food and kindle their fire.' He turned away from me and went to Ali ibn Abi Talib, who was sitting beneath the water-spout of Zamzam, and asked him about *al-'Adiyat dabha*. Ali said: 'Did you ask anyone about it before me?' He said: 'Yes, I asked Ibn Abbas, and he said: they are the horses when they raid in the way of God.' Ali said: 'Go and call him to me.' When I stood over his head, he said: 'You give fatwas to people about what you have no knowledge of! By God, the first military expedition in Islam was Badr, and we had only two horses with us: a horse of al-Zubayr and a horse of al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad. So how can *al-'Adiyat dabha* be horses? *Al-'Adiyat dabha* are from 'Arafah to Muzdalifah, and when they reach Muzdalifah they kindle fires. *Al-Mughirat subha* are from Muzdalifah to Mina, and that is the gathering (jam').' As for His saying ﴿so they raise dust thereby﴾, it is the dust of the earth which they trample with their hooves and their shoes."

Ibn Abbas said: "So I retracted my statement and returned to what Ali had said."

Ibrahim said: "Ali ibn Abi Talib also said: they are the camels."

Ibn Abbas said: "They are the horses." It reached Ali that Ibn Abbas said this, and he said: "We did not have any horses on the day of Badr."

Ibn Abbas said: "That was only in a small expedition (sariyyah) that was dispatched."

Abd ibn Humayd recorded from Amir al-Sha'bi that he said: "Ali and Ibn Abbas disputed about *al-'Adiyat dabha*. Ibn Abbas said: 'They are the horses.' Ali said: 'You lie, O son of Fulanah! By God, there was no rider with us on the day of Badr except al-Miqdad, who was on a piebald horse.'" He said: "And [Ali] used to say: they are the camels. Ibn Abbas said: 'Do you not see that they raise dust? Nothing raises dust except with its hooves.'"

Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from Ali that he said: "The panting of horses is the *hamhamah* (a low neighing), and of camels is the *nafas* (breathing)."

Ibn Asakir recorded from Abu Umamah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding His saying ﴿Indeed, mankind is to his Lord ungrateful (kanud)﴾, that he said: "It means ungrateful (kafur)."

Al-Suyuti graded its chain as weak, and in its chain is Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, who is matruk (abandoned, of disregarded narrations). The mawquf (stopping at the companion) version is more sound, because it did not come through that chain.

Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿And indeed he is, to that, a witness﴾ that he said: "The man." ﴿And indeed he is, in love of wealth, intense﴾: "The wealth."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from him regarding ﴿When what is in the graves is scattered﴾ that he said: "Searched out." ﴿And what is in the breasts is obtained﴾: "Made manifest."

It is Meccan according to the opinion of Ibn Mas'ud, Jabir, al-Hasan, Ikrimah and 'Ata', and Madani according to the opinion of Ibn 'Abbas, Anas ibn Malik and Qatadah.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Surat al-'Adiyat was revealed in Mecca."

Abu 'Ubayd narrated in his Fada'il from al-Hasan who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When al-Zalzalah [i.e., Surat al-Zalzalah] is equal to half the Qur'an, and al-'Adiyat is equal to half the Qur'an." This is a mursal (disconnected) report.

Muhammad ibn Nasr narrated through 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah from Ibn 'Abbas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), a similar report, and he added: "Qul Huwa Allahu Ahad is equal to a third of the Qur'an, and Qul Ya Ayyuha al-Kafirun is equal to a quarter of the Qur'an."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Al-'Adiyat is the plural of 'adiyah, which means that which runs swiftly, from al-'adw, which is walking swiftly. The waw was changed to a ya' because of the kasrah before it, like al-ghaziyat from al-ghazw. What is meant by it is the war horses that run in battle, like running (al-'adw). His saying "dabhan" (ضبحا) is a verbal noun (masdar) emphasizing the active participle, for dabh is a kind of travel and a kind of running. It is said "dabaha al-faras" when the horse runs with force; it is taken from al-dab' (ضبع), which means pushing, and it seems that the ha' is a substitute for the 'ayn.

Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Mubarrad said: dabh comes from the horse stretching its legs (ida'uha) in travel, and from this is the saying of 'Antarah:

"And the horses churn in the pools of death, dabhan"

It may be a masdar in the position of a circumstantial accusative (hal): i.e., dabihat (panting), or possessing dabh. It may also be a masdar of a deleted verb: i.e., they pant a panting. It is said that dabh is the sound of their hooves when they run. Al-Farra' said: dabh is the sound of the horses' breathing when they run.

It is said: they used to muzzle them so that they would not neigh and the enemy would learn of them, so they used to breathe forcefully in this state. It is also said that dabh is a sound heard from the chests of horses when running, which is not neighing (sahil).

The majority has gone to what we mentioned, that the al-'adiyat dabhan are horses. 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, Muhammad ibn Ka'b and al-Suddi said: they are camels, and from this is the saying of Safiyyah bint 'Abd al-Muttalib:

"By the running ones at the gathering of Jam', with their hands, when the dust bursts forth"

The lexicographers reported that the original meaning of dabh belongs to the fox, and it was borrowed for horses. From this is the saying of the poet:

"It pants in the palm like the panting of a fox"

﴿By those that strike sparks by striking﴾ are the horses when they strike fire with their hooves. Al-iraa' is bringing out fire, and al-qadah is striking; the horses' striking with their hooves is made like the striking of flint with steel.

Al-Zajjaj said: when horses run at night and their hooves are struck by stones, sparks fly out of them. The discussion on the accusative of qadhan is like the discussion on the accusative of dabhan, and the disagreement over whether they are horses or camels is like the disagreement mentioned earlier concerning al-'adiyat.

The preponderant view is that they are horses, as the majority held, and as is apparent from the descriptions mentioned in this surah, both what precedes and what follows, for they are clearer in the case of horses than of camels. What differences exist on this among the Companions will come later.

﴿By those that raid at dawn﴾, i.e., those that attack the enemy at morning time. It is said: aghara yughiru ighratan, when he surprises his enemy with killing, capture or plunder. The raiding is attributed to them though it belongs to their people, to indicate that they are their main force in raiding. The accusative of subhan is as an adverb of time.

﴿Then raise thereby a cloud of dust﴾ is coordinated with the verb indicated by the active participle, since the meaning is: those who ran, then they raised; or coordinated with the active participle itself, because it is in the sense of a verb, occurring as a relative clause, for alif and lam in the attributes are relative pronouns. So the sense is: those who ran, then struck fire, then raided, then raised. Al-naq' is the dust they raise against the enemy's face at the time of the raid. Restricting its raising to the morning is because it is the time of the raid, and because the trace of the dust does not appear at night, which is adjacent to the morning.

It is also said that the meaning is: they raised dust in the place of their running, meaning: dust rose or they stirred it up.

The majority read fa-athrna with a light thā' (تخفيف المثلثة). Abu Haywah and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read with shaddah, i.e., they made dust appear thereby.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: al-naq' is raising the voice, and he quoted the verse of Labid:

"So when a true cry is raised, they summon them with jingling and clamour"

He means: when they hear a cry, they rouse the war, i.e., they gather for it.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: and on this I have seen the view of most people of knowledge. End.

But the known meaning among the majority of lexicographers and exegetes is that al-naq' is dust. From this is the saying of the poet:

"They emerge from scattered dust, wounded, as if the tips of their tails were tips of pens"

And the saying of 'Abd Allah ibn Rawahah:

"We would lose our horses if you did not see them stirring dust from the two sides of Kada'"

And the saying of another:

"As if the place of raised dust above our heads and our swords were a night whose stars are falling"

(p-1648) This is what suits the meaning of the verse. Interpreting naq' as sound has little meaning here, for your saying "the horses raided the people of so-and-so at morning and thereby raised a sound" is of little benefit, meaningless, and far from the miraculous eloquence of the Qur'an.

It is also said that al-naq' is the tearing of garments. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: al-naq' is what lies between Muzdalifah and Mina. It is also said it is the bed of the valley.

In al-Sihah: al-naq' is dust, its plural is anqa'; al-naq' is a place where water is held, and likewise what gathers in a well; and al-naq' is land of clayey soil in which water stands.

﴿Then burst thereby into the midst of a host﴾, i.e., they penetrated at that time, or they penetrated, mixed with the dust, into a host of the enemy's hosts, or by their running they came into the midst of the enemy's host. The ba' is either for transitivity, or for circumstance (hal), or is extra. It is said wasatta al-makan: I came to be in its middle. The accusative of jam'an is as its object. The fa's in the four positions indicate the sequence of what follows each one upon what precedes it.

Al-Jumhur read fa-wasatna with a light sin, and it was also read with a shaddah.

When I stood over his head, he said: 'You give fatwas to people about what you have no knowledge of! By God, the first military expedition in Islam was Badr, and we had only two horses with us: a horse of al-Zubayr and a horse of al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad. So how can *al-'Adiyat dabha* be horses? *Al-'Adiyat dabha* are from 'Arafah to Muzdalifah, and when they reach Muzdalifah they kindle fires. *Al-Mughirat subha* are from Muzdalifah to Mina, and that is the gathering (jam').' As for His saying ﴿so they raise dust thereby﴾, it is the dust of the earth which they trample with their hooves and their shoes."

Ibn Abbas said: "So I retracted my statement and returned to what Ali had said."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Ibn Mas'ud regarding ﴿by the chargers, panting﴾ that he said: "They are the camels." They recorded it from him through al-A'mash from Ibrahim al-Nakha'i.

Ibrahim said: "Ali ibn Abi Talib also said: they are the camels."

Ibn Abbas said: "They are the horses." It reached Ali that Ibn Abbas said this, and he said: "We did not have any horses on the day of Badr."

Ibn Abbas said: "That was only in a small expedition (sariyyah) that was dispatched."

Abd ibn Humayd recorded from Amir al-Sha'bi that he said: "Ali and Ibn Abbas disputed about *al-'Adiyat dabha*. Ibn Abbas said: 'They are the horses.' Ali said: 'You lie, O son of Fulanah! By God, there was no rider with us on the day of Badr except al-Miqdad, who was on a piebald horse.'" He said: "And [Ali] used to say: they are the camels. Ibn Abbas said: 'Do you not see that they raise dust? Nothing raises dust except with its hooves.'"

Abd ibn Humayd and al-Hakim, who graded it sound, recorded through Mujahid from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿by the chargers, panting﴾ that he said: "The horses." ﴿Then those who strike sparks﴾: "A man when he strikes his flint." ﴿Then those who raid at dawn﴾: "The horses attacking the enemy at dawn." ﴿So they raise dust thereby﴾: "The dust." ﴿And cleave thereby into the midst of a host﴾: "The enemy."

Abd ibn Humayd recorded from Mujahid regarding ﴿by the chargers, panting﴾ that he said: Ibn Abbas said: "It is fighting." And Ibn Mas'ud said: "It is the Hajj."

Abd al-Razzaq, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded through Amr ibn Dinar from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿by the chargers, panting﴾ that he said: "No animal pants (yadbahu) except the dog or the horse." ﴿Then those who strike sparks﴾: "It is the plotting of a man who strikes and kindles." ﴿Then those who raid at dawn﴾: "The raid of horses at dawn." ﴿So they raise dust thereby﴾: "Dust, the sound of horses' hooves." ﴿And cleave thereby into the midst of a host﴾: "The gathering of the enemy."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿by the chargers, panting﴾ that he said: "The horses. Their panting is their snorting. Do you not see that when the horse runs it says 'ah ah'? That is its panting."

Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from Ali that he said: "The panting of horses is the *hamhamah* (a low neighing), and of camels is the *nafas* (breathing)."

Ibn Jarir recorded from Ibn Mas'ud regarding ﴿by the chargers, panting﴾ that he said: "They are the camels on the Hajj." ﴿Then those who strike sparks﴾: "When they sweep the pebbles with their soles, so that the pebbles strike one another and fire comes out of them." ﴿Then those who raid at dawn﴾: "When they pour forth from Jam'." ﴿So they raise dust thereby﴾: "When they go, they raise the dust."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh recorded through several chains from Ibn Abbas that he said: "*Al-kanud* in our language is the people of the town, the ungrateful one (al-kafur)."

Ibn Asakir recorded from Abu Umamah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding His saying ﴿Indeed, mankind is to his Lord ungrateful (kanud)﴾, that he said: "It means ungrateful (kafur)."

Abd ibn Humayd, al-Bukhari in *al-Adab*, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Mardawayh recorded from Abu Umamah that he said: "The *kanud* is the one who withholds his gift, travels alone, and beats his servant."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Daylami and Ibn Asakir also narrated this from him as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet) report. Al-Suyuti graded its chain as weak, and in its chain is Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, who is matruk (abandoned, of disregarded narrations). The mawquf (stopping at the companion) version is more sound, because it did not come through that chain.

Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿And indeed he is, to that, a witness﴾ that he said: "The man." ﴿And indeed he is, in love of wealth, intense﴾: "The wealth."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from him regarding ﴿When what is in the graves is scattered﴾ that he said: "Searched out." ﴿And what is in the breasts is obtained﴾: "Made manifest."

It is Meccan according to the opinion of Ibn Mas'ud, Jabir, al-Hasan, Ikrimah and 'Ata', and Madani according to the opinion of Ibn 'Abbas, Anas ibn Malik and Qatadah.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Surat al-'Adiyat was revealed in Mecca."

Abu 'Ubayd narrated in his Fada'il from al-Hasan who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When al-Zalzalah [i.e., Surat al-Zalzalah] is equal to half the Qur'an, and al-'Adiyat is equal to half the Qur'an." This is a mursal (disconnected) report.

Muhammad ibn Nasr narrated through 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah from Ibn 'Abbas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), a similar report, and he added: "Qul Huwa Allahu Ahad is equal to a third of the Qur'an, and Qul Ya Ayyuha al-Kafirun is equal to a quarter of the Qur'an."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Al-'Adiyat is the plural of 'adiyah, which means that which runs swiftly, from al-'adw, which is walking swiftly. The waw was changed to a ya' because of the kasrah before it, like al-ghaziyat from al-ghazw. What is meant by it is the war horses that run in battle, like running (al-'adw). His saying "dabhan" (ضبحا) is a verbal noun (masdar) emphasizing the active participle, for dabh is a kind of travel and a kind of running. It is said "dabaha al-faras" when the horse runs with force; it is taken from al-dab' (ضبع), which means pushing, and it seems that the ha' is a substitute for the 'ayn.

Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Mubarrad said: dabh comes from the horse stretching its legs (ida'uha) in travel, and from this is the saying of 'Antarah:

"And the horses churn in the pools of death, dabhan"

It may be a masdar in the position of a circumstantial accusative (hal): i.e., dabihat (panting), or possessing dabh. It may also be a masdar of a deleted verb: i.e., they pant a panting. It is said that dabh is the sound of their hooves when they run. Al-Farra' said: dabh is the sound of the horses' breathing when they run.

It is said: they used to muzzle them so that they would not neigh and the enemy would learn of them, so they used to breathe forcefully in this state. It is also said that dabh is a sound heard from the chests of horses when running, which is not neighing (sahil).

The majority has gone to what we mentioned, that the al-'adiyat dabhan are horses. 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, Muhammad ibn Ka'b and al-Suddi said: they are camels, and from this is the saying of Safiyyah bint 'Abd al-Muttalib:

"By the running ones at the gathering of Jam', with their hands, when the dust bursts forth"

The lexicographers reported that the original meaning of dabh belongs to the fox, and it was borrowed for horses. From this is the saying of the poet:

"It pants in the palm like the panting of a fox"

﴿By those that strike sparks by striking﴾ are the horses when they strike fire with their hooves. Al-iraa' is bringing out fire, and al-qadah is striking; the horses' striking with their hooves is made like the striking of flint with steel.

Al-Zajjaj said: when horses run at night and their hooves are struck by stones, sparks fly out of them. The discussion on the accusative of qadhan is like the discussion on the accusative of dabhan, and the disagreement over whether they are horses or camels is like the disagreement mentioned earlier concerning al-'adiyat.

The preponderant view is that they are horses, as the majority held, and as is apparent from the descriptions mentioned in this surah, both what precedes and what follows, for they are clearer in the case of horses than of camels. What differences exist on this among the Companions will come later.

﴿By those that raid at dawn﴾, i.e., those that attack the enemy at morning time. It is said: aghara yughiru ighratan, when he surprises his enemy with killing, capture or plunder. The raiding is attributed to them though it belongs to their people, to indicate that they are their main force in raiding. The accusative of subhan is as an adverb of time.

﴿Then raise thereby a cloud of dust﴾ is coordinated with the verb indicated by the active participle, since the meaning is: those who ran, then they raised; or coordinated with the active participle itself, because it is in the sense of a verb, occurring as a relative clause, for alif and lam in the attributes are relative pronouns. So the sense is: those who ran, then struck fire, then raided, then raised. Al-naq' is the dust they raise against the enemy's face at the time of the raid. Restricting its raising to the morning is because it is the time of the raid, and because the trace of the dust does not appear at night, which is adjacent to the morning.

It is also said that the meaning is: they raised dust in the place of their running, meaning: dust rose or they stirred it up.

The majority read fa-athrna with a light thā' (تخفيف المثلثة). Abu Haywah and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read with shaddah, i.e., they made dust appear thereby.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: al-naq' is raising the voice, and he quoted the verse of Labid:

"So when a true cry is raised, they summon them with jingling and clamour"

He means: when they hear a cry, they rouse the war, i.e., they gather for it.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: and on this I have seen the view of most people of knowledge. End.

But the known meaning among the majority of lexicographers and exegetes is that al-naq' is dust. From this is the saying of the poet:

"They emerge from scattered dust, wounded, as if the tips of their tails were tips of pens"

And the saying of 'Abd Allah ibn Rawahah:

"We would lose our horses if you did not see them stirring dust from the two sides of Kada'"

And the saying of another:

"As if the place of raised dust above our heads and our swords were a night whose stars are falling"

(p-1648) This is what suits the meaning of the verse. Interpreting naq' as sound has little meaning here, for your saying "the horses raided the people of so-and-so at morning and thereby raised a sound" is of little benefit, meaningless, and far from the miraculous eloquence of the Qur'an.

It is also said that al-naq' is the tearing of garments. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: al-naq' is what lies between Muzdalifah and Mina. It is also said it is the bed of the valley.

In al-Sihah: al-naq' is dust, its plural is anqa'; al-naq' is a place where water is held, and likewise what gathers in a well; and al-naq' is land of clayey soil in which water stands.

﴿Then burst thereby into the midst of a host﴾, i.e., they penetrated at that time, or they penetrated, mixed with the dust, into a host of the enemy's hosts, or by their running they came into the midst of the enemy's host. The ba' is either for transitivity, or for circumstance (hal), or is extra. It is said wasatta al-makan: I came to be in its middle. The accusative of jam'an is as its object. The fa's in the four positions indicate the sequence of what follows each one upon what precedes it.

Al-Jumhur read fa-wasatna with a light sin, and it was also read with a shaddah.

﴿Indeed, mankind is ungrateful to his Lord﴾. This is the answer to the oath. What is meant by mankind is some of its members, namely the disbeliever. Al-kanud is one who is ungrateful for blessings. His saying "li-rabbihi" (to his Lord) is connected to kanud, and was placed first for the sake of the rhyme (ri'ayat al-fawasil). From this is the saying of the poet:

"Ungrateful toward the favours of men, and whoever is ungrateful toward the favours of men will be far"

i.e., ungrateful for the favours of men. It is said he is one who denies the truth; it is said that Kindah was so named because it denied its father.

It is also said that kanud is derived from kanad, which is cutting, as if he cut off what he should have kept connected of gratitude. It is said: kanada al-habl, when he cut the rope, and from this is the saying of al-A'sha:

"The joining of ropes and their cutting"

It is also said: al-kanud is the miser, and Abu Zayd recited:

"Indeed my soul has not been pleased with you, a soul, except that I am left with a debt that is ungrateful"

It is also said: al-kanud is the envious, and it is said the ignorant of his own worth. Interpreting kanud as ungrateful for blessings is more fitting to the context, and one who denies blessings is an unbeliever in them; the rest of what has been said does not suit the context.

﴿And indeed he is, to that, a witness﴾, i.e., indeed mankind, in his ingratitude, is a witness, testifying against himself by it, because its effect is apparent upon him. It is also said the meaning is: indeed Allah, may His praise be exalted, is a witness to that from the son of Adam. The majority held this.

Al-Hasan, Qatadah and Muhammad ibn Ka'b held the first view.

And it is more preponderant than the view of the majority, because of His saying: ﴿And indeed he is, in love of wealth, intense﴾, for the pronoun refers to mankind. The meaning: indeed he is, in love of wealth, strong, diligent in seeking and acquiring it, and absorbed in it. It is said: he is intense (shadid) for this matter and strong for it when he is capable of it. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If he leaves wealth (khayr)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 180], and from this is the saying of 'Adi ibn Hatim:

"What do souls hope for from seeking the good, and love of life is its liar"

It is also said: the meaning is: indeed mankind, because of love of wealth, is stingy. The first is preferable.

The lam in al-hubb is connected to shadid.

Ibn Zayd said: Allah called wealth "good" (khayr), though it may be evil, but people find it good, so He called it good.

Al-Farra' said: the original structure of the verse would be: "indeed he is intensely loving of the good," like His saying: ﴿On a stormy day﴾ [Ibrahim: 18], where stormy belongs to the wind, not the day; as if He said: on a day stormy for the wind.

﴿Does he not know that when what is in the graves is scattered﴾. The interrogative is for denial, and the fa' is for coordination upon an implied element required by the context: i.e., he does what he does of ugly deeds and yet does not know. Ba'thara means nathara and bahatha: i.e., what is in the graves of the dead is scattered and searched, and they are brought out.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: ba'thartu al-mata'a: I made its bottom its top.

Al-Farra' said: I heard some Arabs of Banu Asad say: bahthara, with ha' in place of 'ayn. This has been discussed before in His saying: ﴿And when the graves are scattered﴾ [al-Infitar: 4].

﴿And what is in the breasts is made apparent﴾, i.e., what is in them of good and evil is distinguished and clarified. Tahsil is distinguishing, so said the exegetes. It is also said: hussila means: uburiza (brought forth).

Al-Jumhur read hussila with a damma on the ha' and a shaddah on the sad, kasrah, in passive form. 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Yahya ibn Ya'mar and Nasr ibn 'Asim read hasala with fatha on the ha' and sad, lightened, in active form: i.e., it became apparent.

﴿Indeed their Lord, concerning them, that Day, is All-Aware﴾, i.e., indeed the Lord of those who are resurrected, concerning them, is All-Aware; nothing of them is hidden from Him, so He will recompense them: good for good, and evil for evil.

Al-Zajjaj said: Allah is aware of them on that day and on other days, but the meaning is: Allah will recompense them for their disbelief on that day. Similar is His saying: ﴿Those are they whom Allah knows what is in their hearts﴾ [al-Nisa': 63], meaning: those whose recompense Allah does not neglect.

Al-Jumhur read inna rabbahum with a kasrah on the hamzah and the lam in khabir. Abu al-Simak read with a fatha on the hamzah and dropped the lam from khabir.

Al-Bazzar, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Daraqutni in al-Afrad, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent out horsemen, and their news was delayed for a month, and no report came to him from them; so Allah revealed: ﴿By the running ones, panting (dabhan)﴾ — they panted with their feet." The wording of Ibn Mardawayh: they panted with their nostrils.

﴿By those that strike sparks by striking﴾: they struck stones with their hooves and brought forth fire. ﴿By those that raid at dawn﴾: they attacked the people at morning with a raid. ﴿Then raise thereby a cloud of dust﴾: they raised dust with their hooves. ﴿Then burst thereby into the midst of a host﴾: they attacked the whole people at morning.

Dabh is the snorting of horses when they snort.

﴿By those that strike sparks by striking﴾ — he said: when the horses run, they strike fire as their hooves hit stones. ﴿By those that raid at dawn﴾ — he said: they are horses that raided, attacking the enemy at morning. ﴿Then raise thereby a cloud of dust﴾ — he said: they are horses that raised dust with their hooves, meaning by the running of horses; and al-naq' is dust. ﴿Then burst thereby into the midst of a host﴾ — he said: the host is the enemy.

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Abu Salih who said: I disputed with Ikrimah concerning the meaning of al-'adiyat. He said: Ibn 'Abbas said: they are horses in battle, and their panting is when they loosen their muzzles as they run. ﴿By those that strike sparks by striking﴾ — he said: they make the polytheists see their plot. ﴿By those that raid at dawn﴾ — he said: when they attack the enemy at morning. ﴿Then burst thereby into the midst of a host﴾ — he said: when they penetrate the middle of the enemy.

Abu Salih said: So I said: 'Ali said: they are camels in the pilgrimage, and my master was more knowing than your master.

The majority read fa-athrna with a light thā' (تخفيف المثلثة). Abu Haywah and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read with shaddah, i.e., they made dust appear thereby.

"So when a true cry is raised, they summon them with jingling and clamour"

He means: when they hear a cry, they rouse the war, i.e., they gather for it.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: and on this I have seen the view of most people of knowledge. End.

But the known meaning among the majority of lexicographers and exegetes is that al-naq' is dust. From this is the saying of the poet:

And the saying of 'Abd Allah ibn Rawahah:

And the saying of another:

Abu 'Ubaydah said: ba'thartu al-mata'a: I made its bottom its top.

Similar is His saying: ﴿Those are they whom Allah knows what is in their hearts﴾ [al-Nisa': 63], meaning: those whose recompense Allah does not neglect.

Dabh is the snorting of horses when they snort.

﴿By those that strike sparks by striking﴾ — he said: when the horses run, they strike fire as their hooves hit stones. ﴿By those that raid at dawn﴾ — he said: they are horses that raided, attacking the enemy at morning. ﴿Then raise thereby a cloud of dust﴾ — he said: they are horses that raised dust with their hooves, meaning by the running of horses; and al-naq' is dust. ﴿Then burst thereby into the midst of a host﴾ — he said: the host is the enemy.

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Abu Salih who said: I disputed with Ikrimah concerning the meaning of al-'adiyat. He said: Ibn 'Abbas said: they are horses in battle, and their panting is when they loosen their muzzles as they run. ﴿By those that strike sparks by striking﴾ — he said: they make the polytheists see their plot. ﴿By those that raid at dawn﴾ — he said: when they attack the enemy at morning. ﴿Then burst thereby into the midst of a host﴾ — he said: when they penetrate the middle of the enemy.

Abu Salih said: So I said: 'Ali said: they are camels in the pilgrimage, and my master was more knowing than your master.

The commentator (al-Shawkani) cites Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Anbari in *Kitab al-Adداد* (the Book of Opposites), and al-Hakim, who graded it sound, and Ibn Mardawayh, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "While I was sitting in the Hijr, a man came to me and asked about *al-'Adiyat dabha* (﴿the chargers, panting﴾). I said: 'They are the horses when they raid in the way of God, then they return at night, and they prepare their food and kindle their fire.' He turned away from me and went to Ali ibn Abi Talib, who was sitting beneath the water-spout of Zamzam, and asked him about *al-'Adiyat dabha*. Ali said: 'Did you ask anyone about it before me?' He said: 'Yes, I asked Ibn Abbas, and he said: they are the horses when they raid in the way of God.' Ali said: 'Go and call him to me.' When I stood over his head, he said: 'You give fatwas to people about what you have no knowledge of! By God, the first military expedition in Islam was Badr, and we had only two horses with us: a horse of al-Zubayr and a horse of al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad. So how can *al-'Adiyat dabha* be horses? *Al-'Adiyat dabha* are from 'Arafah to Muzdalifah, and when they reach Muzdalifah they kindle fires. *Al-Mughirat subha* are from Muzdalifah to Mina, and that is the gathering (jam').' As for His saying ﴿so they raise dust thereby﴾, it is the dust of the earth which they trample with their hooves and their shoes."

Ibn Abbas said: "So I retracted my statement and returned to what Ali had said."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded from Ibn Mas'ud regarding ﴿by the chargers, panting﴾ that he said: "They are the camels." They recorded it from him through al-A'mash from Ibrahim al-Nakha'i.

Ibrahim said: "Ali ibn Abi Talib also said: they are the camels."

Ibn Abbas said: "They are the horses." It reached Ali that Ibn Abbas said this, and he said: "We did not have any horses on the day of Badr."

Ibn Abbas said: "That was only in a small expedition (sariyyah) that was dispatched."

Abd ibn Humayd recorded from Amir al-Sha'bi that he said: "Ali and Ibn Abbas disputed about *al-'Adiyat dabha*. Ibn Abbas said: 'They are the horses.' Ali said: 'You lie, O son of Fulanah! By God, there was no rider with us on the day of Badr except al-Miqdad, who was on a piebald horse.'" He said: "And [Ali] used to say: they are the camels. Ibn Abbas said: 'Do you not see that they raise dust? Nothing raises dust except with its hooves.'"

Abd ibn Humayd and al-Hakim, who graded it sound, recorded through Mujahid from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿by the chargers, panting﴾ that he said: "The horses." ﴿Then those who strike sparks﴾: "A man when he strikes his flint." ﴿Then those who raid at dawn﴾: "The horses attacking the enemy at dawn." ﴿So they raise dust thereby﴾: "The dust." ﴿And cleave thereby into the midst of a host﴾: "The enemy."

Abd ibn Humayd recorded from Mujahid regarding ﴿by the chargers, panting﴾ that he said: Ibn Abbas said: "It is fighting." And Ibn Mas'ud said: "It is the Hajj."

Abd al-Razzaq, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded through Amr ibn Dinar from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿by the chargers, panting﴾ that he said: "No animal pants (yadbahu) except the dog or the horse." ﴿Then those who strike sparks﴾: "It is the plotting of a man who strikes and kindles." ﴿Then those who raid at dawn﴾: "The raid of horses at dawn." ﴿So they raise dust thereby﴾: "Dust, the sound of horses' hooves." ﴿And cleave thereby into the midst of a host﴾: "The gathering of the enemy."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿by the chargers, panting﴾ that he said: "The horses. Their panting is their snorting. Do you not see that when the horse runs it says 'ah ah'? That is its panting."

Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from Ali that he said: "The panting of horses is the *hamhamah* (a low neighing), and of camels is the *nafas* (breathing)."

Ibn Jarir recorded from Ibn Mas'ud regarding ﴿by the chargers, panting﴾ that he said: "They are the camels on the Hajj." ﴿Then those who strike sparks﴾: "When they sweep the pebbles with their soles, so that the pebbles strike one another and fire comes out of them." ﴿Then those who raid at dawn﴾: "When they pour forth from Jam'." ﴿So they raise dust thereby﴾: "When they go, they raise the dust."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh recorded through several chains from Ibn Abbas that he said: "*Al-kanud* in our language is the people of the town, the ungrateful one (al-kafur)."

Ibn Asakir recorded from Abu Umamah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding His saying ﴿Indeed, mankind is to his Lord ungrateful (kanud)﴾, that he said: "It means ungrateful (kafur)."

Abd ibn Humayd, al-Bukhari in *al-Adab*, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Mardawayh recorded from Abu Umamah that he said: "The *kanud* is the one who withholds his gift, travels alone, and beats his servant."

Al-Suyuti graded its chain as weak, and in its chain is Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, who is matruk (abandoned, of disregarded narrations). The mawquf (stopping at the companion) version is more sound, because it did not come through that chain.

Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿And indeed he is, to that, a witness﴾ that he said: "The man." ﴿And indeed he is, in love of wealth, intense﴾: "The wealth."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from him regarding ﴿When what is in the graves is scattered﴾ that he said: "Searched out." ﴿And what is in the breasts is obtained﴾: "Made manifest."

It is Meccan according to the opinion of Ibn Mas'ud, Jabir, al-Hasan, Ikrimah and 'Ata', and Madani according to the opinion of Ibn 'Abbas, Anas ibn Malik and Qatadah.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Surat al-'Adiyat was revealed in Mecca."

Abu 'Ubayd narrated in his Fada'il from al-Hasan who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When al-Zalzalah [i.e., Surat al-Zalzalah] is equal to half the Qur'an, and al-'Adiyat is equal to half the Qur'an." This is a mursal (disconnected) report.

Muhammad ibn Nasr narrated through 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah from Ibn 'Abbas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), a similar report, and he added: "Qul Huwa Allahu Ahad is equal to a third of the Qur'an, and Qul Ya Ayyuha al-Kafirun is equal to a quarter of the Qur'an."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

It is said: he is intense (shadid) for this matter and strong for it when he is capable of it. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If he leaves wealth (khayr)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 180], and from this is the saying of 'Adi ibn Hatim:

It is also said: the meaning is: indeed mankind, because of love of wealth, is stingy. The first is preferable.

Ibn Zayd said: Allah called wealth "good" (khayr), though it may be evil, but people find it good, so He called it good.

Al-Farra' said: the original structure of the verse would be: "indeed he is intensely loving of the good," like His saying: ﴿On a stormy day﴾ [Ibrahim: 18], where stormy belongs to the wind, not the day; as if He said: on a day stormy for the wind.

﴿Does he not know that when what is in the graves is scattered﴾. The interrogative is for denial, and the fa' is for coordination upon an implied element required by the context: i.e., he does what he does of ugly deeds and yet does not know. Ba'thara means nathara and bahatha: i.e., what is in the graves of the dead is scattered and searched, and they are brought out.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: ba'thartu al-mata'a: I made its bottom its top.

Al-Jumhur read hussila with a damma on the ha' and a shaddah on the sad, kasrah, in passive form. 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Yahya ibn Ya'mar and Nasr ibn 'Asim read hasala with fatha on the ha' and sad, lightened, in active form: i.e., it became apparent.

﴿Indeed their Lord, concerning them, that Day, is All-Aware﴾, i.e., indeed the Lord of those who are resurrected, concerning them, is All-Aware; nothing of them is hidden from Him, so He will recompense them: good for good, and evil for evil.

Similar is His saying: ﴿Those are they whom Allah knows what is in their hearts﴾ [al-Nisa': 63], meaning: those whose recompense Allah does not neglect.

Al-Jumhur read inna rabbahum with a kasrah on the hamzah and the lam in khabir. Abu al-Simak read with a fatha on the hamzah and dropped the lam from khabir.

Al-Bazzar, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Daraqutni in al-Afrad, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent out horsemen, and their news was delayed for a month, and no report came to him from them; so Allah revealed: ﴿By the running ones, panting (dabhan)﴾ — they panted with their feet." The wording of Ibn Mardawayh: they panted with their nostrils.

﴿By those that strike sparks by striking﴾: they struck stones with their hooves and brought forth fire. ﴿By those that raid at dawn﴾: they attacked the people at morning with a raid. ﴿Then raise thereby a cloud of dust﴾: they raised dust with their hooves. ﴿Then burst thereby into the midst of a host﴾: they attacked the whole people at morning.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated through another route from him, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent a detachment against the enemy, and its news was delayed, which grieved him; so Allah informed him of their news and what had happened to them, and He said: ﴿By the running ones, panting (dabhan)﴾ — he said: they are horses."

Dabh is the snorting of horses when they snort.

﴿By those that strike sparks by striking﴾ — he said: when the horses run, they strike fire as their hooves hit stones. ﴿By those that raid at dawn﴾ — he said: they are horses that raided, attacking the enemy at morning. ﴿Then raise thereby a cloud of dust﴾ — he said: they are horses that raised dust with their hooves, meaning by the running of horses; and al-naq' is dust. ﴿Then burst thereby into the midst of a host﴾ — he said: the host is the enemy.

Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Abu Salih who said: I disputed with Ikrimah concerning the meaning of al-'adiyat. He said: Ibn 'Abbas said: they are horses in battle, and their panting is when they loosen their muzzles as they run. ﴿By those that strike sparks by striking﴾ — he said: they make the polytheists see their plot. ﴿By those that raid at dawn﴾ — he said: when they attack the enemy at morning. ﴿Then burst thereby into the midst of a host﴾ — he said: when they penetrate the middle of the enemy.

Abu Salih said: So I said: 'Ali said: they are camels in the pilgrimage, and my master was more knowing than your master.

The commentator (al-Shawkani) cites Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Anbari in *Kitab al-Adداد* (the Book of Opposites), and al-Hakim, who graded it sound, and Ibn Mardawayh, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "While I was sitting in the Hijr, a man came to me and asked about *al-'Adiyat dabha* (﴿the chargers, panting﴾). I said: 'They are the horses when they raid in the way of God, then they return at night, and they prepare their food and kindle their fire.' He turned away from me and went to Ali ibn Abi Talib, who was sitting beneath the water-spout of Zamzam, and asked him about *al-'Adiyat dabha*. Ali said: 'Did you ask anyone about it before me?' He said: 'Yes, I asked Ibn Abbas, and he said: they are the horses when they raid in the way of God.' Ali said: 'Go and call him to me.' When I stood over his head, he said: 'You give fatwas to people about what you have no knowledge of! By God, the first military expedition in Islam was Badr, and we had only two horses with us: a horse of al-Zubayr and a horse of al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad. So how can *al-'Adiyat dabha* be horses? *Al-'Adiyat dabha* are from 'Arafah to Muzdalifah, and when they reach Muzdalifah they kindle fires. *Al-Mughirat subha* are from Muzdalifah to Mina, and that is the gathering (jam').' As for His saying ﴿so they raise dust thereby﴾, it is the dust of the earth which they trample with their hooves and their shoes."

Ibn Abbas said: "So I retracted my statement and returned to what Ali had said."

Ibrahim said: "Ali ibn Abi Talib also said: they are the camels."

Ibn Abbas said: "They are the horses." It reached Ali that Ibn Abbas said this, and he said: "We did not have any horses on the day of Badr."

Ibn Abbas said: "That was only in a small expedition (sariyyah) that was dispatched."

Abd ibn Humayd recorded from Amir al-Sha'bi that he said: "Ali and Ibn Abbas disputed about *al-'Adiyat dabha*. Ibn Abbas said: 'They are the horses.' Ali said: 'You lie, O son of Fulanah! By God, there was no rider with us on the day of Badr except al-Miqdad, who was on a piebald horse.'" He said: "And [Ali] used to say: they are the camels. Ibn Abbas said: 'Do you not see that they raise dust? Nothing raises dust except with its hooves.'"

Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from Ali that he said: "The panting of horses is the *hamhamah* (a low neighing), and of camels is the *nafas* (breathing)."

The mawquf (stopping at the companion) version is more sound, because it did not come through that chain.

It is Meccan according to the opinion of Ibn Mas'ud, Jabir, al-Hasan, Ikrimah and 'Ata', and Madani according to the opinion of Ibn 'Abbas, Anas ibn Malik and Qatadah.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Surat al-'Adiyat was revealed in Mecca."

Abu 'Ubayd narrated in his Fada'il from al-Hasan who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When al-Zalzalah [i.e., Surat al-Zalzalah] is equal to half the Qur'an, and al-'Adiyat is equal to half the Qur'an." This is a mursal (disconnected) report.

Muhammad ibn Nasr narrated through 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah from Ibn 'Abbas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), a similar report, and he added: "Qul Huwa Allahu Ahad is equal to a third of the Qur'an, and Qul Ya Ayyuha al-Kafirun is equal to a quarter of the Qur'an."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Al-'Adiyat is the plural of 'adiyah, which means that which runs swiftly, from al-'adw, which is walking swiftly. The waw was changed to a ya' because of the kasrah before it, like al-ghaziyat from al-ghazw. What is meant by it is the war horses that run in battle, like running (al-'adw). His saying "dabhan" (ضبحا) is a verbal noun (masdar) emphasizing the active participle, for dabh is a kind of travel and a kind of running. It is said "dabaha al-faras" when the horse runs with force; it is taken from al-dab' (ضبع), which means pushing, and it seems that the ha' is a substitute for the 'ayn.

Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Mubarrad said: dabh comes from the horse stretching its legs (ida'uha) in travel, and from this is the saying of 'Antarah:

"And the horses churn in the pools of death, dabhan"

It may be a masdar in the position of a circumstantial accusative (hal): i.e., dabihat (panting), or possessing dabh. It may also be a masdar of a deleted verb: i.e., they pant a panting. It is said that dabh is the sound of their hooves when they run. Al-Farra' said: dabh is the sound of the horses' breathing when they run.

It is said: they used to muzzle them so that they would not neigh and the enemy would learn of them, so they used to breathe forcefully in this state. It is also said that dabh is a sound heard from the chests of horses when running, which is not neighing (sahil).

The majority has gone to what we mentioned, that the al-'adiyat dabhan are horses. 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, Muhammad ibn Ka'b and al-Suddi said: they are camels, and from this is the saying of Safiyyah bint 'Abd al-Muttalib:

"By the running ones at the gathering of Jam', with their hands, when the dust bursts forth"

The lexicographers reported that the original meaning of dabh belongs to the fox, and it was borrowed for horses. From this is the saying of the poet:

"It pants in the palm like the panting of a fox"

﴿By those that strike sparks by striking﴾ are the horses when they strike fire with their hooves. Al-iraa' is bringing out fire, and al-qadah is striking; the horses' striking with their hooves is made like the striking of flint with steel.

Al-Zajjaj said: when horses run at night and their hooves are struck by stones, sparks fly out of them. The discussion on the accusative of qadhan is like the discussion on the accusative of dabhan, and the disagreement over whether they are horses or camels is like the disagreement mentioned earlier concerning al-'adiyat.

The preponderant view is that they are horses, as the majority held, and as is apparent from the descriptions mentioned in this surah, both what precedes and what follows, for they are clearer in the case of horses than of camels. What differences exist on this among the Companions will come later.

﴿By those that raid at dawn﴾, i.e., those that attack the enemy at morning time. It is said: aghara yughiru ighratan, when he surprises his enemy with killing, capture or plunder. The raiding is attributed to them though it belongs to their people, to indicate that they are their main force in raiding. The accusative of subhan is as an adverb of time.

﴿Then raise thereby a cloud of dust﴾ is coordinated with the verb indicated by the active participle, since the meaning is: those who ran, then they raised; or coordinated with the active participle itself, because it is in the sense of a verb, occurring as a relative clause, for alif and lam in the attributes are relative pronouns. So the sense is: those who ran, then struck fire, then raided, then raised. Al-naq' is the dust they raise against the enemy's face at the time of the raid. Restricting its raising to the morning is because it is the time of the raid, and because the trace of the dust does not appear at night, which is adjacent to the morning.

It is also said that the meaning is: they raised dust in the place of their running, meaning: dust rose or they stirred it up.

The majority read fa-athrna with a light thā' (تخفيف المثلثة). Abu Haywah and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read with shaddah, i.e., they made dust appear thereby.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: al-naq' is raising the voice, and he quoted the verse of Labid:

"So when a true cry is raised, they summon them with jingling and clamour"

He means: when they hear a cry, they rouse the war, i.e., they gather for it.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: and on this I have seen the view of most people of knowledge. End.

But the known meaning among the majority of lexicographers and exegetes is that al-naq' is dust. From this is the saying of the poet:

"They emerge from scattered dust, wounded, as if the tips of their tails were tips of pens"

And the saying of 'Abd Allah ibn Rawahah:

"We would lose our horses if you did not see them stirring dust from the two sides of Kada'"

And the saying of another:

"As if the place of raised dust above our heads and our swords were a night whose stars are falling"

(p-1648) This is what suits the meaning of the verse. Interpreting naq' as sound has little meaning here, for your saying "the horses raided the people of so-and-so at morning and thereby raised a sound" is of little benefit, meaningless, and far from the miraculous eloquence of the Qur'an.

It is also said that al-naq' is the tearing of garments. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: al-naq' is what lies between Muzdalifah and Mina. It is also said it is the bed of the valley.

In al-Sihah: al-naq' is dust, its plural is anqa'; al-naq' is a place where water is held, and likewise what gathers in a well; and al-naq' is land of clayey soil in which water stands.

﴿Then burst thereby into the midst of a host﴾, i.e., they penetrated at that time, or they penetrated, mixed with the dust, into a host of the enemy's hosts, or by their running they came into the midst of the enemy's host. The ba' is either for transitivity, or for circumstance (hal), or is extra. It is said wasatta al-makan: I came to be in its middle. The accusative of jam'an is as its object. The fa's in the four positions indicate the sequence of what follows each one upon what precedes it.

Al-Jumhur read fa-wasatna with a light sin, and it was also read with a shaddah.

﴿Indeed, mankind is ungrateful to his Lord﴾. This is the answer to the oath. What is meant by mankind is some of its members, namely the disbeliever. Al-kanud is one who is ungrateful for blessings. His saying "li-rabbihi" (to his Lord) is connected to kanud, and was placed first for the sake of the rhyme (ri'ayat al-fawasil). From this is the saying of the poet:

"Ungrateful toward the favours of men, and whoever is ungrateful toward the favours of men will be far"

i.e., ungrateful for the favours of men. It is said he is one who denies the truth; it is said that Kindah was so named because it denied its father.

It is also said that kanud is derived from kanad, which is cutting, as if he cut off what he should have kept connected of gratitude. It is said: kanada al-habl, when he cut the rope, and from this is the saying of al-A'sha:

"The joining of ropes and their cutting"

It is also said: al-kanud is the miser, and Abu Zayd recited:

"Indeed my soul has not been pleased with you, a soul, except that I am left with a debt that is ungrateful"

It is also said: al-kanud is the envious, and it is said the ignorant of his own worth. Interpreting kanud as ungrateful for blessings is more fitting to the context, and one who denies blessings is an unbeliever in them; the rest of what has been said does not suit the context.

Abd ibn Humayd recorded from Amir al-Sha'bi that he said: "Ali and Ibn Abbas disputed about *al-'Adiyat dabha*. Ibn Abbas said: 'They are the horses.' Ali said: 'You lie, O son of Fulanah! By God, there was no rider with us on the day of Badr except al-Miqdad, who was on a piebald horse.'" He said: "And [Ali] used to say: they are the camels. Ibn Abbas said: 'Do you not see that they raise dust? Nothing raises dust except with its hooves.'"

Abd ibn Humayd and al-Hakim, who graded it sound, recorded through Mujahid from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿by the chargers, panting﴾ that he said: "The horses." ﴿Then those who strike sparks﴾: "A man when he strikes his flint." ﴿Then those who raid at dawn﴾: "The horses attacking the enemy at dawn." ﴿So they raise dust thereby﴾: "The dust." ﴿And cleave thereby into the midst of a host﴾: "The enemy."

Abd ibn Humayd recorded from Mujahid regarding ﴿by the chargers, panting﴾ that he said: Ibn Abbas said: "It is fighting." And Ibn Mas'ud said: "It is the Hajj."

Abd al-Razzaq, Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim recorded through Amr ibn Dinar from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿by the chargers, panting﴾ that he said: "No animal pants (yadbahu) except the dog or the horse." ﴿Then those who strike sparks﴾: "It is the plotting of a man who strikes and kindles." ﴿Then those who raid at dawn﴾: "The raid of horses at dawn." ﴿So they raise dust thereby﴾: "Dust, the sound of horses' hooves." ﴿And cleave thereby into the midst of a host﴾: "The gathering of the enemy."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿by the chargers, panting﴾ that he said: "The horses. Their panting is their snorting. Do you not see that when the horse runs it says 'ah ah'? That is its panting."

Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from Ali that he said: "The panting of horses is the *hamhamah* (a low neighing), and of camels is the *nafas* (breathing)."

Ibn Jarir recorded from Ibn Mas'ud regarding ﴿by the chargers, panting﴾ that he said: "They are the camels on the Hajj." ﴿Then those who strike sparks﴾: "When they sweep the pebbles with their soles, so that the pebbles strike one another and fire comes out of them." ﴿Then those who raid at dawn﴾: "When they pour forth from Jam'." ﴿So they raise dust thereby﴾: "When they go, they raise the dust."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh recorded through several chains from Ibn Abbas that he said: "*Al-kanud* in our language is the people of the town, the ungrateful one (al-kafur)."

Ibn Asakir recorded from Abu Umamah, from the Prophet (ﷺ), regarding His saying ﴿Indeed, mankind is to his Lord ungrateful (kanud)﴾, that he said: "It means ungrateful (kafur)."

Abd ibn Humayd, al-Bukhari in *al-Adab*, al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Mardawayh recorded from Abu Umamah that he said: "The *kanud* is the one who withholds his gift, travels alone, and beats his servant."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Daylami and Ibn Asakir also narrated this from him as a marfu' (traced to the Prophet) report. Al-Suyuti graded its chain as weak, and in its chain is Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, who is matruk (abandoned, of disregarded narrations). The mawquf (stopping at the companion) version is more sound, because it did not come through that chain.

Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from Ibn Abbas regarding ﴿And indeed he is, to that, a witness﴾ that he said: "The man." ﴿And indeed he is, in love of wealth, intense﴾: "The wealth."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir recorded from him regarding ﴿When what is in the graves is scattered﴾ that he said: "Searched out." ﴿And what is in the breasts is obtained﴾: "Made manifest."

It is Meccan according to the opinion of Ibn Mas'ud, Jabir, al-Hasan, Ikrimah and 'Ata', and Madani according to the opinion of Ibn 'Abbas, Anas ibn Malik and Qatadah.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Surat al-'Adiyat was revealed in Mecca."

Abu 'Ubayd narrated in his Fada'il from al-Hasan who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When al-Zalzalah [i.e., Surat al-Zalzalah] is equal to half the Qur'an, and al-'Adiyat is equal to half the Qur'an." This is a mursal (disconnected) report.
